parts.article:
Caral: an ancient South American city
 
(A) Huge earth and rock mounds rise out of the desert of the Supe Valley near the coast of Peru in South America. These immense mounds appear simply to be part of the geographical landscape in this arid region squeezed between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes mountains. But looks deceive. These are actually human-made pyramids. Strong evidence indicates they are the remains of a city known as Caral that flourished nearly 5,000 years ago. If true, it would be the oldest known urban center in the Americas and among the most ancient in the world. Research undertaken by Peruvian archaeologist Ruth Shady suggests that the 150-acre complex of pyramids, plazas and residential buildings was a thriving metropolis when Egypt’s great pyramids were still being built. Though discovered in 1905, for years Caral attracted little attention, largely because archaeologists believed the structures were fairly recent. But the monumental scale of the pyramids had long interested Shady, who began excavations at the site in 1996, about 22 kilometers from the coast and 190 kilometers north of Peru’s capital city of Lima.
 
(B) Shady and her crew searched for broken remains of the pots and containers that most such sites contain. Not finding any only made her more excited; it meant Caral could be what archaeologists term pre-ceramic, that is, existing before the advent in the area of pot-firing techniques. Shady’s team undertook the task of excavating Piramide Mayor, the largest of the pyramids. After carefully clearing away many hundreds of years’ worth of rubble and sand, they identified staircases, walls covered with remnants of colored woven bags and brickwork. In the foundations, they found the remains of grass-like reeds woven into bags. The original workers, she surmised, must have filled these bags with stones from a nearby quarry and laid them atop one another inside retaining walls, gradually giving rise to the pyramid’s immense structure. Shady had samples of the reeds subjected to radiocarbon dating and found that the reeds were 4,600 years old. This evidence indicated that Caral was, in fact, more than 1,000 years older than what had previously been thought to be the oldest urban center in the Americas.
 
(C) What amazed archaeologists was not just the age, but the complexity and scope of Caral. Piramide Mayor alone covers an area nearly the size of four football fields and is 18 meters tall. A nine-meter-wide staircase rises from a circular plaza at the foot of the pyramid, passing over three terraced levels until it reaches the top. Thousands of manual laborers would have been needed to build such a project, not counting the many architects, craftsmen, and managers. Shady’s team found the remains of a large amphitheater, containing almost 70 musical instruments made of bird and deer bones. Clearly, music played an important role in Caral’s society. Around the perimeter of Caral are a series of smaller mounds and various buildings. These indicate a hierarchy of living arrangements: large, well-kept rooms atop pyramids for the elite, ground-level quarters for craftsmen, and shabbier outlying dwellings for workers.
 
(D) But why had Caral been built in the first place? Her excavations convinced Shady that Caral once served as a trade center for the region, which extends from the rainforests of the Amazon to the high forests of the Andes. Shady found evidence of a rich trading environment, including seeds of the cocoa bush and necklaces of shells, neither of which was native to the immediate Caral area. This environment gave rise to people who did not take part in the production of food, allowing them to become priests and planners, builders and designers. Thus occupational specialization, elemental to an urban society, emerged.
 
(E) But what sustained such a trading center and drew travelers to it? Was it food? Shady and her team found the bones of small edible fish, which must have come from the Pacific coast to the west, in the excavations. But they also found evidence of squash, sweet potatoes and beans having been grown locally. Shady theorized that Caral’s early farmers diverted the area’s rivers into canals, which still cross the Supe Valley today, to irrigate their fields. But because she found no traces of maize, which can be traded or stored and used in times of crop failure, she concluded that Caral’s trade leverage was not based on stockpiling food supplies. It was evidence of another crop in the excavations that gave Shady the best clue to Caral’s success. In nearly every excavated building, her team discovered evidence of cotton—seeds, fibers and textiles. Her theory fell into place when a large fishing net made of those fibers, unearthed in an unrelated dig on Peru’s coast, turned out to be as old as Caral. “The farmers of Caral grew the cotton that the fishermen needed to make their nets,” Shady speculates. “And the fishermen gave them shellfish and dried fish in exchange for these nets.” In essence, the people of Caral enabled fishermen to work with larger and more effective nets, which made the resources of the sea more readily available, and the fishermen probably used dried squash grown by the Caral people as flotation devices for their nets.
parts.questions:
Questions 1–6
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 1–6 on your answer sheet, write:

Q1 Caral was built at the same time as the construction of the Egyptian pyramids.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q2 The absence of pottery at the archaeological dig gave Shady a significant clue to the age of the site.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q3 The stones used to build Piramide Mayor came from a location far away.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q4 The huge and complicated structures of Piramide Mayor suggest that its construction required an organised team of builders.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q5 Archaeological evidence shows that the residents of Caral were highly skilled musicians.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q6 The remains of housing areas at Caral suggest that there were no class distinctions in residential areas.

  • A TRUE
  • B FALSE
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 7–13
Complete the notes below.
Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 7–13 on your answer sheet.
Caral as a trading centre
Items discovered at Caral but not naturally occurring in the area

reference:
Q1

干扰 “Was a thriving metropolis”（已建成并繁荣的状态） vs “still being built”（正在建造的动作）。前者先于后者，反驳了“at the same time”。

句子 (Paragraph A) “...Caral... was a thriving metropolis when Egypt’s great pyramids were still being built.”

解析 题目说卡拉尔是在埃及金字塔建造的同一时期建造的。原文A段指出，当埃及大金字塔“were still being built（还在建造中）”时，卡拉尔已经是“thriving metropolis（繁荣的大都市）”了。这说明卡拉尔的建造完成并达到繁荣的时间早于埃及金字塔的建造期，两者并非“同时建造（built at the same time）”，时间线上有先后之分，故选 FALSE。

Q2

解析 题目说考古挖掘中陶器的缺失给了Shady关于该遗址年代的重要线索。原文B段提到Shady没有找到破碎的罐子（Not finding any），这意味着卡拉尔可能是“pre-ceramic（前陶器时代的）”，即存在于陶器烧制技术出现之前，这直接提供了关于其古老年代的线索，选 TRUE。

干扰 “Absence of pottery” 对应 “Not finding any (pots and containers)”，“Clue to the age” 对应 “meant Caral could be... pre-ceramic... existing before...”。

句子 (Paragraph B) “Not finding any only made her more excited; it meant Caral could be what archaeologists term pre-ceramic...”

Q3

解析 题目说建造Piramide Mayor的石头来自很远的地方。原文B段提到工人们用来自“nearby quarry（附近的采石场）”的石头装满袋子，nearby（附近的）直接反驳了 far away（很远的），选 FALSE。

干扰 地点状语矛盾：nearby vs far away。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...filled these bags with stones from a nearby quarry...”

Q4

干扰 “Organised team” 对应原文列举的各类分工角色（architects, craftsmen, managers）。

解析 题目说Piramide Mayor巨大且复杂的结构表明其建造需要一个有组织的建筑团队。原文C段提到建造这样的项目需要数千名体力劳动者，更不用说许多“architects, craftsmen, and managers（建筑师、工匠和管理者）”，这种分工明确的人员构成显然描述了一个有组织的团队，选 TRUE。

句子 (Paragraph C) “Thousands of manual laborers ... not counting the many architects, craftsmen, and managers.”

Q5

解析 题目说考古证据表明Caral的居民是**技艺高超的（highly skilled）**音乐家。原文C段只提到发现了近70种乐器，且音乐在社会中扮演重要角色，但并未评价居民的演奏水平是否“highly skilled”，信息缺失，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 “Found instruments（发现乐器）” 推不出 “Highly skilled musicians（技艺高超）”。

句子 (Paragraph C) “...containing almost 70 musical instruments... music played an important role...”

Q6

解析 题目说Caral的住房区域遗迹表明居住区没有阶级区分。原文C段末尾明确指出这些建筑表明了“hierarchy of living arrangements（居住安排的等级制度）”：精英在塔顶大房间，工匠在地面，工人在简陋的外围住所。有等级即有阶级区分，直接反驳题目，选 FALSE。

干扰 “No class distinctions” 与原文的 “hierarchy（等级）” 截然相反。

句子 (Paragraph C) “These indicate a hierarchy of living arrangements...”

Q7

句子 (Paragraph D) “...including seeds of the cocoa bush...”

干扰 “Of a certain plant” 对应 “of the cocoa bush”。

解析 题目说某种植物的____。原文D段提到发现了丰富的贸易环境证据，包括可可灌木的“seeds（种子）”，填 seeds。

Q8

解析 题目说用于制作珠宝的____。原文D段提到“necklaces of shells（贝壳项链）”，项链属于珠宝（jewellery），填 shells。

干扰 “Used to make jewellery” 对应 “necklaces of...”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “...and necklaces of shells...”

Q9

解析 题目说某种食物的残骸，如____。原文E段提到发现了小食用“fish（鱼）”的骨头，填 fish。

干扰 “Remains of certain food” 对应 “bones of small edible fish”。

句子 (Paragraph E) “...the bones of small edible fish...”

Q10

句子 (Paragraph E) “...diverted the area’s rivers into canals, which still cross the Supe Valley today...”

解析 题目说今天仍然存在的____表明水从河流中引出。原文E段提到早期的农民将河流引入“canals（运河/水渠）”，这些运河今天仍然穿过Supe山谷（still cross... today），填 canals。

干扰 “Still in existence today” 对应 “still cross the Supe Valley today”。

Q11

解析 题目说没有证据表明种植了____。原文E段说因为她发现了“no traces of maize（没有玉米的痕迹）”，填 maize。

干扰 “No evidence that... was grown” 对应 “found no traces of...”。

句子 (Paragraph E) “But because she found no traces of maize...”

Q12

解析 题目说挖掘发现和海岸上的渔网表明Caral农民交易了____。原文E段末尾提到Caral农民种植了渔民需要的“cotton（棉花）”来做网，并进行交换，填 cotton。

干扰 “Traded” 对应原文语境中的 “grew... that the fishermen needed... in exchange for”。

句子 (Paragraph E) “The farmers of Caral grew the cotton that the fishermen needed...”

Q13

解析 题目说干南瓜可能被用来辅助渔网的____。原文E段最后一句提到渔民可能使用Caral人种的干南瓜作为渔网的“flotation devices（漂浮装置）”，填 flotation。

干扰 “Aid ______ of fishing nets” 对应 “as flotation devices for their nets”。

句子 (Paragraph E) “...used dried squash... as flotation devices for their nets.”
